title: Structure-Token Evidence-Anchored Reasoning for Scientific Chart Understanding
abstract: Scientific charts encode quantities in axes, legends, and geometric marks, yet large vision-language models still treat them as natural photographs. Visual in-context examples do not expose the coordinate frame; unconstrained chain-of-thought can name a plausible number that was never read from a bar. We present STEER (Structure-Token Evidence-anchored Reasoning), which freezes a Llama-3.2-Vision encoder and inserts three modules: a chart structure graph encoder (CSGE) that binds ticks, legend items, and marks; evidence-anchored step reasoning (EASR) that forces every arithmetic step to cite a graph node; and weak-parser strong-reasoner alignment (WPSR) that uses a specialized table extractor only as a teacher of node attributes. On ChartQA, STEER reaches 82.70 average relaxed accuracy versus 80.16 for ChartGemma and 76.40 for a LLaVA-CoT backbone trained on the same mix. Gains widen on CharXiv reasoning (33.60 vs. 29.20 InternVL Chat V1.5) and ChartQAPro CoT (40.70 vs. 37.17 Qwen2-VL-7B), where OCR shortcuts disappear. Ablations show that dropping node serialization or numeric candidate constraints undoes most of the reasoning lift.

title: Conditional Timed Partial Orders: An Expressive and Interpretable Framework for Robot Task Specification and Planning
abstract: Timed Partial Orders (TPOs), originally proposed for workflows, provide an interpretable framework for robot task specification with planning algorithms based on mixed-integer linear programming (MILP). However, TPOs are limited in expressivity, capturing only partial-order events with simple timing constraints. In this paper, we introduce Conditional TPOs (cTPOs), which extend TPOs with richer relative-timing constraints and conditional event activations based on environmental conditions. We show that planning for cTPOs also reduces to an MILP problem; however, the added expressivity results in significantly larger MILPs that can become computationally intractable. To address this challenge, we propose a decomposition algorithm that partitions a cTPO into smaller sub-TPOs, yielding a sequence of smaller MILP problems. We prove that this decomposition is complete and preserves plan optimality while improving the interpretability of complex tasks. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of cTPOs as a task specification framework and the efficiency of our decomposition approach, achieving up to four orders of magnitude speedup over the monolithic MILP.

title: Flow3D-OPD: Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation for 3D Geometry Generation with Flow-Matching Diffusion Transformer
abstract: Recent image-to-3D generation models built on flow-matching diffusion Transformers (DiT) can produce high-fidelity meshes, yet their post-training strategy remains largely unexplored. There exist several critical bottlenecks in reinforcement learning: the inherent difficulty of defining comprehensive rewards for 3D geometric quality, and the gradient interference that arises when jointly optimizing heterogeneous objectives. Inspired by the practicability of on-policy distillation (OPD) in large language models and image generation, we propose \textbf{Flow3D-OPD}, a two-stage post-training framework that introduces multi-teacher distillation into 3D geometry generation. In the first stage, we utilize the semi-policy to enhance the foundational capability of the pretrained model and then design an agentic verifier for 3D geometric quality evaluation. Based on the verifier, we could cultivate domain-specialized teacher models via direct preference optimization (DPO). In the second stage, we consolidate heterogeneous expertise into a unified student model through on-policy distillation with hard task-routing sampling and gradient accumulation, which could mitigate the gradient interference in joint optimization. Without relying on elaborate modifications, our straightforward yet effective design achieves consistent improvements across all geometric quality dimensions and surpasses all teacher models in the average metric. evidence.title: Flow3D-OPD: Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation for 3D Geometry Generation with Flow-Matching Diffusion Transformer
evidence.abstract: Recent image-to-3D generation models built on flow-matching diffusion Transformers (DiT) can produce high-fidelity meshes, yet their post-training strategy remains largely unexplored. There exist several critical bottlenecks in reinforcement learning: the inherent difficulty of defining comprehensive rewards for 3D geometric quality, and the gradient interference that arises when jointly optimizing heterogeneous objectives. Inspired by the practicability of on-policy distillation (OPD) in large language models and image generation, we propose \textbf{Flow3D-OPD}, a two-stage post-training framework that introduces multi-teacher distillation into 3D geometry generation. Based on the verifier, we could cultivate domain-specialized teacher models via direct preference optimization (DPO). In the second stage, we consolidate heterogeneous expertise into a unified student model through on-policy distillation with hard task-routing sampling and gradient accumulation, which could mitigate the gradient interference in joint optimization. Without relying on elaborate modifications, our straightforward yet effective design achieves consistent improvements across all geometric quality dimensions and surpasses all teacher models in the average metric. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach provides an effective paradigm for reinforcement learning in 3D generation.

title: Deep Learning for Biopsy-Free Subtyping of Basal Cell Carcinoma from Dermatoscopic Images
abstract: Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC) is the most common type of skin cancer, accounting for nearly 80% of skin cancer di- agnoses. Its optimal clinical management is guided by the distinct histopathologic subtype, with aggressive variants requiring more drastic measures. In current clinical practice, subtyping relies on skin biopsies, a procedure both costly and invasive. In this paper, we conduct a preliminary investigation into using deep learning for BCC subtyping, solely from a single dermatoscopic image of the lesion. Given the limited data at our disposal, we employ pre-trained vision transformers (ViTs), a state-of-the-art family of models highly effective for challenging downstream tasks with limited labeled data. Through repeated stratified k-fold cross-validation, we demonstrate that ViTs can achieve superior performance (AUC 0.784 on a dataset of 1271 dermatoscopic images of various BCC subtypes) over standard CNN-based baselines as well as previously-reported human reader perfor- mance, on the task of differentiating aggressive BCCs from other subtype families. These initial findings highlight the potential of combining deep learning and dermatoscopy to provide a biopsy- free alternative for BCC subtyping, thus aiding in improving treatment planning and patient outcomes.

title: Supplementary Code and Census Artifacts for "Quadratic relations of differentially 4-uniform permutations: a sharp displacement bound and an orbit-equivariant census"
abstract: This repository contains the computational artifacts, replication code, and census datasets accompanying the research paper: "Quadratic relations of differentially 4-uniform permutations: a sharp displacement bound and an orbit-equivariant census" by Ilhom Abdurazzokov. Abstract:The AES S-box is the multiplicative inverse on GF(2^8) composed with an affine map, and it pays for its optimal (NL, DU) = (112, 4) with algebraic structure: exactly 39 linearly independent quadratic relations. This work investigates what it costs to give some of that structure up and characterizes the exact bounds. Writing Q(F) for the quadratic relation count and d_H for the Hamming distance from the inverse map, we prove that Q is 1-Lipschitz in d_H and characterize when the bound is attained. The archive includes:- Complete enumeration and verification scripts for the d_H <= 4 neighborhood (including the 1,573,133,760 permutations at d_H = 4).- Orbit-equivariant census data for permutations commuting with multiplicative subgroup C (|C| = 85 and |C| = 51 families).- Evaluation pipelines for quadratic relation counts (Q), differential uniformity (DU), nonlinearity (NL), and boomerang uniformity (beta).

title: Dynamic Neural Networks: Adaptive Neuron Connectivity
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic neural network architecture that employs adaptive neuron connections to dynamically adjust the strength of connections based on the input data's dynamic changes. Traditional neural network models often rely on static connections, limiting their adaptability and potential for improved performance. Our proposed mechanism leverages iterative learning to automatically tune the connection weights, resulting in a more efficient and robust neural network. This work addresses the limitations of static models by enabling the network to respond intelligently to evolving data patterns. The resulting network demonstrates improved generalization capabilities and enhanced performance across a range of benchmark datasets.

title: 基于自组织网络的非线性几何模型优化器
abstract: This paper introduces a novel optimization algorithm based on a self-organizing network to refine geometric models. Traditional optimization methods often struggle with complex, non-linear models, and the inherent noise in the optimization process can lead to suboptimal solutions. This work leverages the self-organizing network's ability to iteratively refine parameters through a process of exploration and exploitation, resulting in improved model precision and generalization capabilities. The algorithm employs a modified reinforcement learning approach, incorporating a reward function that prioritizes model accuracy while considering the network's structure, fostering a dynamic and adaptable optimization process. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach through a series of simulations, showcasing significant improvements in model convergence and accuracy compared to traditional methods.

title: Dynamic Neuron Topology Mapping and Adaptive Neuron Connection Generation
abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework for dynamically mapping neuron topologies and generating adaptive neuron connections within neural networks. The core idea is to integrate topological network modeling with reinforcement learning to create a system capable of learning and adapting to complex neural network topologies. The system employs a multi-level modeling approach. The first level utilizes topological networks such as small-world networks and scale-free networks to represent the neural network. The second level leverages reinforcement learning algorithms, such as policy gradient or Actor-Critic, to train the connection strength between neurons. Crucially, connection strength is determined not only by neuron input/output activity but also by local topological information, including connection density and distance. A third level, an adaptive topology generation module, dynamically alters the topology structure based on network performance and learning objectives, adding or removing neurons and modifying their connections. This approach aims to optimize information processing and learning efficiency by mitigating information bottlenecks and accelerating signal propagation. The system demonstrates the potential to overcome limitations of existing neural network modeling methods and address complex learning and information processing challenges in neural networks.

title: Probability Geometric Systems for Logical Revelation and High-Order Inference
abstract: Probability Geometric Systems (PGS) presents a novel approach to logical revelation and high-order inference by integrating probability logic geometry with the principles of set theory reversal. This system leverages the inherent properties of probability events to automatically discover hidden logical relationships and structures within data sets. The core mechanism centers around a dynamic, iterative process of event generation, logical deduction, and set-theoretic analysis, effectively uncovering patterns and dependencies that would otherwise remain hidden. This research proposes a framework for constructing a system capable of performing sophisticated reasoning, including the identification of complex relationships and the generation of novel insights. The significance of PGS lies in its potential to surpass traditional methods by embracing probabilistic reasoning and offering a more intuitive and automated approach to logical exploration.

title: Self-Organizing Fractal Neural Networks for Pattern Recognition
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to pattern recognition utilizing self-organizing fractal neural networks. The core idea is to leverage the inherent hierarchical structure of fractals to create networks that are both efficient and adaptable. We propose an evolutionary algorithm that iteratively refines the fractal network's topology, optimizing it for a specific pattern recognition task. The algorithm's guidance is based on a feedback mechanism that continuously assesses pattern recognition accuracy. Through this process, the network dynamically adjusts its fractal structure, leading to improved performance compared to traditional, static neural network architectures. This research demonstrates a promising pathway for developing intelligent systems capable of robust and adaptable pattern recognition in complex environments. The key mathematical formulations and concepts presented in this paper contribute to a deeper understanding of this emerging field.

title: Algorithmic Randomness Generation via Quantum Walks
abstract: The generation of true randomness remains a significant challenge in computer science, particularly when relying solely on classical algorithms. Many current approaches employ pseudo-random number generators (PRNGs), which, despite their computational efficiency, are inherently predictable and lack genuine randomness. This paper proposes a novel method for algorithmic randomness generation leveraging the principles of quantum walks. We demonstrate that the inherent uncertainty and superposition properties of quantum systems provide a robust mechanism for generating truly random numbers. Specifically, we outline a framework for designing quantum walks on graphs, where the evolution of the walker's state is fundamentally probabilistic and unpredictable. The core of our approach resides in exploiting the quantum walk's non-deterministic nature to produce sequences of numbers that exhibit statistical properties consistent with true randomness. The theoretical framework is presented, including a detailed description of the mathematical formalism underlying the quantum walk and the probability distribution of the walker's positions. We highlight the potential advantages of this approach, particularly in scenarios demanding high-quality randomness for cryptographic applications or simulations. The key concept is to translate a classical problem into a quantum one, where the inherent probabilistic nature of quantum mechanics offers a superior solution to the problem of generating genuine randomness.

title: Phase-Field Optimization - Dynamical Constraint Optimization of Complex Systems
abstract: Phase-field optimization represents a novel approach to dynamic optimization, offering a robust method for optimizing complex systems by iteratively adjusting parameters based on the current state. This paper explores the core principles of this technique, detailing the algorithm's implementation, its advantages over existing methods, and its potential applications in various fields. We delve into the importance of defining constraints and the iterative adjustment process to achieve optimal results. The focus is on demonstrating the effectiveness of the phase-field approach through a concrete example, showcasing its ability to handle complex scenarios with dynamic constraints. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions, aiming to further refine the algorithm and expand its applicability.

title: Quantum Memory Mechanism in Quantum Error Correction Networks
abstract: This paper proposes a novel "quantum memory" mechanism within quantum error correction (QEC) networks, leveraging continuous-time error correction codes and the nonlinear properties of superconducting quantum interference devices (SQUIDs). The core claim is the design of a system capable of storing and retrieving past quantum states, significantly enhancing the overall resilience and performance of QEC networks. The mechanism utilizes an engineered "quantum memory" built within an SQUID, allowing for the controlled storage and replay of quantum state information generated during error correction processes. Unlike conventional QEC codes limited to single-shot corrections, this approach incorporates historical data for optimized error mitigation. Mathematical formulations detailing the core concepts and operational parameters are presented, illustrating the potential for improved error correction rates and extended coherence times in QEC networks. This research contributes a fundamental shift in QEC methodology, moving beyond sequential correction to a dynamic, state-aware approach.

title: Adam: Open Representation Birth, Compositional Theory Selection, and Auditable Scientific Rediscovery Based on Dual-Level CAF-VGCTG
abstract: Abstract Existing AI systems for scientific discovery mainly focus on recovering expressions, parameters, or structures within predefined candidate spaces from observational data. A more difficult question is whether, when the target scientific representation itself is not explicitly supplied, an AI system can reorganize existing but fragmented knowledge and autonomously form a higher-level anonymous representation; at the same time, whether an older representation that remains persistently incompatible with the new evidence structure can naturally lose qualification through evidence-driven compositional failure, rather than because the researcher has rewarded the target answer in advance. We introduce Adam, an auditable scientific-reasoning architecture and benchmark based on Dual-level Cross-Area Fusion VGCTG (DCAFVGCTG). The architecture separates six classes of mechanisms that are otherwise easily conflated: directional eligibility, cross-area conditional superposition, long-term law-relation memory, recoverable graph abstraction, representation composition/anonymous birth, and downstream execution correction. The first CAF level permits conditional transfer only from lower-curvature to higher-curvature regions according to dynamically reconstructed curvature ordering. The second CAF level is defined as a true recoverable Graph Loss operator (L_G), which compresses admissible multistep structures into higher-level abstract relations while retaining an archive capable of reconstructing the source path. SEC acts only on execution weights after the structure has been determined and is not permitted to alter curvature-direction topology, CAF topology, or the abstract graph. Adam is built on the earlier VGCTG architecture, as instantiated in the frozen second-generation VRCTG/VDRCTG implementation VRCTG_VDRCTG_v3_0_FROZEN1 (hereafter GMv3), but does not replace VGCTG’s existing relation- and direction-governance mechanisms. VGCTG already distinguishes the latent law relation (R_{ij}^{\mathrm{law}}), current data reliability (G_i^{\mathrm{data}}), instantaneous lower-to-higher directional eligibility (A_{ij}^{\kappa}), and actual execution weight (P_{ij}^{\mathrm{exec}}), and uses relation compatibility, persistent incompatibility, dormancy, and retraction to govern whether local candidates remain eligible to share a law. Adam adds representation-level structural composability above this relation layer. For scientifically distinct representations such as ether, scalar, vector, and metric-like representations, an artificial numerical concept distance such as (d(\mathrm{ether},\mathrm{metric})) cannot be naturally defined. Representation survival is therefore determined by whether heterogeneous evidence can be composed into a closed, compressive, recoverable, and predictively capable structure. In the strongest experiment, metric is completely removed from the proposal space. The system may use only existing non-target representations and anonymous latent variables (z_k). Anonymous representations are first born independently and are only afterward evaluated through a common post-hoc characterization ledger to determine whether they possess metric-like properties. For the normalized preferred-frame ether competitor, insufficient evidence permits only dormancy; actual retraction requires both persistent compositional failure and reliable contradiction in an independent paired blind region. Thus, “excluding ether” and “forming a metric-like representation” are two independent mechanism chains. In the frozen 701:730 block, 28 of 30 seeds formed anonymous representations, of which 3 were subsequently characterized as metric-like and simultaneously satisfied the predefined Adam-0 conditions. All three passed the field-equation gate and completed independent tensor and weak-field audits. In the one-time independent confirmation block 801:830, 24/30 seeds produced anonymous representations, of which 2 formed metric-like Adam-0 events. Across the five authorized events, the byte-locked field-equation assembler consistently recovered a Ricci + (Rg) structure with (b/a) close to (-1/2), while the weak-field coupling remained near (2.076\times10^{-43}). Destroying the conservation ledger or the weak-field ledger counterfactually disrupted the corresponding tensor ratio or coupling. No seed without a metric-like anonymous representation was permitted to activate the field-equation assembler. In the subsequent frozen FEv4 independent-confirmation block 1001:1030, the real arm produced anonymous representations in 22/30 seeds, with 1/30 satisfying both metric-like Birth and Adam-0 criteria. The corresponding metric-like Birth and Adam-0 counts were both 2/30 in the cross-edge arm; the paired exact comparison of metric-like emergence rates gave p=1. Cross-edge interventions were validly applied in 9/30 seeds and reached the audited Birth input in 5/30 seeds, whereas the GL source-evidence arm produced no valid composition-changing sample. These results extend the independent-block observation of Adam-0 but establish neither a success-rate advantage over the cross-edge null nor the effect of effective GL evidence reassociation. In the subsequent separate block 1701:1730, FEv5 v0.7 applied two-dimensional priority selection after qualification: common DECISION predictive improvement first, qualified BirthScore second. Across six paired arms, input-concept challenge C and dual-source governance D each achieved Adam-0 and governed Adam-0 in 2/30 seeds, compared with 1/30 in original arm A, output-side arm B, budget control E, and common-lifecycle control F. All five prespecified Adam-0 paired comparisons had exact and Holm-adjusted (p) values of 1; the corresponding governed comparisons also had exact (p) values of 1. The increased counts therefore do not establish a statistically significant success-rate advantage. C and D had identical success counts despite mean search trials of 14 and 72, respectively, with no additional observed success rate in D. The FEv4 cross-edge arm had already reached 2/30; cross-block counts are not used to estimate the effects of anti-intuition or priority selection. These results do not constitute an independent discovery of general relativity by AI from a “no-knowledge” condition. The stricter conclusion is that, within a frozen, auditable benchmark that isolates the target label while intentionally retaining structured physical priors, an unnamed higher-order scientific representation can naturally emerge from fragmented knowledge, while an older representation that persistently fails to compose the evidence can lose qualification through an independent evidence chain. We call this minimal phenomenon Adam-0 and characterize the present result as auditable constrained scientific rediscovery. evidence.title: Adam: Open Representation Birth, Compositional Theory Selection, and Auditable Scientific Rediscovery Based on Dual-Level CAF-VGCTG
evidence.abstract: Abstract Existing AI systems for scientific discovery mainly focus on recovering expressions, parameters, or structures within predefined candidate spaces from observational data. A more difficult question is whether, when the target scientific representation itself is not explicitly supplied, an AI system can reorganize existing but fragmented knowledge and autonomously form a higher-level anonymous representation; at the same time, whether an older representation that remains persistently incompatible with the new evidence structure can naturally lose qualification through evidence-driven compositional failure, rather than because the researcher has rewarded the target answer in advance. We introduce Adam, an auditable scientific-reasoning architecture and benchmark based on Dual-level Cross-Area Fusion VGCTG (DCAFVGCTG). The architecture separates six classes of mechanisms that are otherwise easily conflated: directional eligibility, cross-area conditional superposition, long-term law-relation memory, recoverable graph abstraction, representation composition/anonymous birth, and downstream execution correction. The first CAF level permits conditional transfer only from lower-curvature to higher-curvature regions according to dynamically reconstructed curvature ordering. The second CAF level is defined as a true recoverable Graph Loss operator (L_G), which compresses admissible multistep structures into higher-level abstract relations while retaining an archive capable of reconstructing the source path. SEC acts only on execution weights after the structure has been determined and is not permitted to alter curvature-direction topology, CAF topology, or the abstract graph. Adam is built on the earlier VGCTG architecture, as instantiated in the frozen second-generation VRCTG/VDRCTG implementation VRCTG_VDRCTG_v3_0_FROZEN1 (hereafter GMv3), but does not replace VGCTG’s existing relation- and direction-governance mechanisms. VGCTG already distinguishes the latent law relation (R_{ij}^{\mathrm{law}}), current data reliability (G_i^{\mathrm{data}}), instantaneous lower-to-higher directional eligibility (A_{ij}^{\kappa}), and actual execution weight (P_{ij}^{\mathrm{exec}}), and uses relation compatibility, persistent incompatibility, dormancy, and retraction to govern whether local candidates remain eligible to share a law. Adam adds representation-level structural composability above this relation layer. For scientifically distinct representations such as ether, scalar, vector, and metric-like representations, an artificial numerical concept distance such as (d(\mathrm{ether},\mathrm{metric})) cannot be naturally defined. Representation survival is therefore determined by whether heterogeneous evidence can be composed into a closed, compressive, recoverable, and predictively capable structure. In the strongest experiment, metric is completely removed from the proposal space. The system may use only existing non-target representations and anonymous latent variables (z_k). Anonymous representations are first born independently and are only afterward evaluated through a common post-hoc characterization ledger to determine whether they possess metric-like properties. For the normalized preferred-frame ether competitor, insufficient evidence permits only dormancy; actual retraction requires both persistent compositional failure and reliable contradiction in an independent paired blind region. Thus, “excluding ether” and “forming a metric-like representation” are two independent mechanism chains. In the frozen 701:730 block, 28 of 30 seeds formed anonymous representations, of which 3 were subsequently characterized as metric-like and simultaneously satisfied the predefined Adam-0 conditions. All three passed the field-equation gate and completed independent tensor and weak-field audits. In the one-time independent confirmation block 801:830, 24/30 seeds produced anonymous representations, of which 2 formed metric-like Adam-0 events. Across the five authorized events, the byte-locked field-equation assembler consistently recovered a Ricci + (Rg) structure with (b/a) close to (-1/2), while the weak-field coupling remained near (2.076\times10^{-43}). Destroying the conservation ledger or the weak-field ledger counterfactually disrupted the corresponding tensor ratio or coupling. No seed without a metric-like anonymous representation was permitted to activate the field-equation assembler. In the subsequent frozen FEv4 independent-confirmation block 1001:1030, the real arm produced anonymous representations in 22/30 seeds, with 1/30 satisfying both metric-like Birth and Adam-0 criteria. The corresponding metric-like Birth and Adam-0 counts were both 2/30 in the cross-edge arm; the paired exact comparison of metric-like emergence rates gave p=1. Cross-edge interventions were validly applied in 9/30 seeds and reached the audited Birth input in 5/30 seeds, whereas the GL source-evidence arm produced no valid composition-changing sample. These results extend the independent-block observation of Adam-0 but establish neither a success-rate advantage over the cross-edge null nor the effect of effective GL evidence reassociation. In the subsequent separate block 1701:1730, FEv5 v0.7 applied two-dimensional priority selection after qualification: common DECISION predictive improvement first, qualified BirthScore second. Across six paired arms, input-concept challenge C and dual-source governance D each achieved Adam-0 and governed Adam-0 in 2/30 seeds, compared with 1/30 in original arm A, output-side arm B, budget control E, and common-lifecycle control F. All five prespecified Adam-0 paired comparisons had exact and Holm-adjusted (p) values of 1; the corresponding governed comparisons also had exact (p) values of 1. The increased counts therefore do not establish a statistically significant success-rate advantage. C and D had identical success counts despite mean search trials of 14 and 72, respectively, with no additional observed success rate in D. The FEv4 cross-edge arm had already reached 2/30; cross-block counts are not used to estimate the effects of anti-intuition or priority selection. These results do not constitute an independent discovery of general relativity by AI from a “no-knowledge” condition. The stricter conclusion is that, within a frozen, auditable benchmark that isolates the target label while intentionally retaining structured physical priors, an unnamed higher-order scientific representation can naturally emerge from fragmented knowledge, while an older representation that persistently fails to compose the evidence can lose qualification through an independent evidence chain. We call this minimal phenomenon Adam-0 and characterize the present result as auditable constrained scientific rediscovery. title: Discriminability-Aware Symmetric Bit-Wise Feature Encoding for Resource-Constrained IoT Traffic Classification
abstract: Resource-constrained traffic classification requires mapping heterogeneous numerical features into a fixed-length binary input. Equal-width encoding ignores differences in discriminability, whereas range-only allocation may spend precision on weak predictors. We propose discriminability-aware symmetric bit-wise feature encoding (DA-SBFE), which combines training-fold mutual information with a robust numerical range to allocate tiered feature precision under a fixed budget. P4-programmable SmartNICs serve as a deployment-oriented case study because constrained per-packet processing motivates compact, deterministic representations. We do not claim hardware deployment. On 83,868 packets from the official UNSW IoT traces, DA-SBFE with BNN-Large achieved 0.9330 ± 0.0019 macro-F1 at 256 bits versus 0.9185 ± 0.0020 for Range-SBFE, with positive differences in all five folds. The gain increased from 0.0144 at 256 bits to 0.0348 at 192 bits and 0.0556 at 128 bits, and remained at 0.0176 after removing port features. Cross-day transfer showed only a small positive mean difference (0.0032) with mixed seed-level directions, so stable temporal robustness was not established. Deterministic integer XNOR–popcount inference matched PyTorch for all 16,774 held-out packets. The evidence supports DA-SBFE as a software-validated encoding method. Compilation, resource-use measurement, throughput evaluation, and latency evaluation remain future work.

title: Ant colony mapping for dimensionality reduction to discrete spaces
abstract: Dimensionality reduction is a widely used technique in AI with various application areas. It maps feature vectors of high dimension to a space of lower dimension so that the new representation maintains some meaningful properties of the original data (i.e., similar vectors have similar new representations). This paper considers the problem of dimensionality reduction to discrete spaces. A novel distributed, stochastic ’swarm intelligence’ algorithm, Ant Colony Mapping (ACOM), is proposed to generate approximate solutions to the problem. ACOM is a generalisation of the brood-sorting behaviour of certain ant species that results in the spatial clustering of objects. After demonstrating ACOM’s basic behaviour, the algorithm’s performance on 2D lattice topologies is analysed in terms of the number of ants and the number of problem parameters. The performance is compared to that of a recent, local search-enhanced Steady-State Genetic Algorithm, namely Steady-State Memetic Algorithm (SSMA), as a baseline, both in terms of solution quality and computational budget. Additional experiments compare ACOM, an annealed variant, and an LAS-ACOM hybrid with non-evolutionary grid-sorting baselines on a random-RGB benchmark. Annealing and hybridisation improve ACOM’s alignment quality, but global baselines remain stronger; in exchange, ACOM uses local operations with constant complexity rather than the cubic complexity of assignment-based methods.

title: Abstention Errors and Segment Support in CUAD: An Auditable Contract-Extraction Case Study
abstract: Contract-clause extraction benchmarks measure reference recovery, but interpreting a system for review assistance also requires measuring unnecessary output and the evidence available within categories. This paper presents a retrospective, reproducible evaluation of a fixed public RoBERTa checkpoint on CUAD's published 102-contract test split. Candidate generation is preserved from an earlier frozen run; matching errors are corrected and category thresholds are reselected on 62 training-split contracts using the original 90% recall target. The corrected operating point recovers 82.2% of reference spans at 8.2% CUAD precision. Of 30,464 returned candidate strings, 19,562 occur on questions with no annotated answer. The system answers 1,335 of 2,938 such questions, a 45.4% false-positive rate (95% contract-bootstrap interval: 43.3-47.9%). Matching candidates constitute 20.3% of returned strings, illustrating why reference-based precision and candidate-level review burden require different denominators. Only nine of 41 categories have at least 30 positive and 30 negative contracts; this count changes to 18 and two under support minima of 20 and 40. Two categories have no negative contracts, making their no-answer false-positive rates undefined. These findings describe one checkpoint, decoder, and threshold policy. Earlier test access and uncertain checkpoint training overlap limit confirmatory interpretation. The paper supplies the original and corrected analyses, predictions, and software checks as ancillary artifacts; it establishes neither a new release criterion nor production readiness.

title: Toward Fault-Tolerant Variational Optimization: QAOA under [[4,2,2]] Error Detection
abstract: We present a partially fault-tolerant implementation of QAOA based on the $[[4,2,2]]$ error-detection code, targeting the Max-Cut problem on a square graph. Our main contribution is a novel ancilla-mediated logical $R_{ZZ}$ gate enabling interactions between qubits in different $[[4,2,2]]$ blocks. We evaluate unencoded and encoded circuits under five noise models, with both all-to-all and grid-routed connectivity, using the Cirq and qsimcirq frameworks with parallel CPU execution. Post-selection on stabilizer measurements consistently improves the probability of sampling optimal bitstrings, with five measurements providing the strongest benefit. These results support error-detection as a practical near-term strategy for improving the quality of variational quantum algorithms.

title: AFID: A Unified Open Framework for Automated Fingermark Identification, Quality Assessment and Feature Extraction
abstract: Automated fingermark identification is the foundation of forensic investigation, yet progress in the field is held back by fragmented, closed-source solutions trained on private or discontinued data. We present AFID, a unified open-source framework for friction ridge image processing that performs recognition, quality assessment, and feature extraction based on a single shared encoder, trained exclusively on publicly available data. At its core is a fixed-length representation learned for identity discrimination, trained under heavy augmentation. Despite applying essentially no preprocessing beyond resizing and padding at inference, AFID sets a new state of the art in fixed-length fingermark recognition, leading identification across NIST SD 27 (67.6% rank-1) , SD 302 (54.9% rank-1), and SD 303 (67.6% rank-1), surpassing a commercial matcher on fingermarks. From the same frozen backbone, a quality assessment module predicts recognition utility more accurately than any compared baseline and generalizes across independent matchers, while lightweight decoders recover minutiae, ridge orientation, and segmentation competitive with dedicated methods. The framework proves that a single, efficiently trained encoder can support the full fingermark processing pipeline, from recognition through quality assessment all the way to feature extraction. To accelerate research on fingermark analysis even further, we release the code, models, and annotations to the community.

title: NutriBench-Kitchen: Benchmarking Embodied AI for Nutrition Management
abstract: An embodied kitchen assistant must do more than recognize food in isolated frames. It must track ingredient states over time and integrate visual observations with recipe and nutritional knowledge to support constraint-aware decision-making. We formalize this capability as \emph{Embodied Nutrition Management}: perceiving nutrition-relevant events, maintaining a persistent food state, and using it for knowledge-grounded planning. Existing benchmarks evaluate static food understanding or embodied cooking actions, but do not measure whether an agent can continuously update and use nutrition-relevant states in dynamic kitchens. To fill this gap, we introduce \textbf{NutriBench-Kitchen}, a benchmark containing 1,500 manually verified question--answer pairs from 160 cooking videos. It covers five task families: Ingredient Entry, Memory Management, Recipe Query, Long-Term Planning, and Short-Term Planning, spanning food-state construction, maintenance, knowledge retrieval, and decision-making across different planning horizons. Evaluations of proprietary and open-source large vision-language models reveal a substantial gap from human performance, particularly in quantitative ingredient estimation, long-term state tracking, and reasoning under interacting constraints. We further introduce \textbf{Nutri-Vgent}, a diagnostic long-video agent with separate episodic, food-state, and recipe memories. Its consistent improvements demonstrate the value of explicit state representations and structured memory for nutrition management. Together, NutriBench-Kitchen and Nutri-Vgent provide a testbed for studying persistent state tracking and knowledge-grounded reasoning in dynamic kitchens. Code is available at https://github.com/V1ol1n/NutriBench-Kitchen.

title: Learning Adaptive SED for heterogeneous load balancing
abstract: We study a two-server load balancing system with heterogeneous service rates that are a priori unknown to the dispatcher. The goal is to route customers according to the Shortest--Expected--Delay (SED) policy, but this requires knowledge of the service rates. Empirical policies that route based on estimates perform poorly: due to estimation error, the empirical policy disagrees with the oracle on an infinite region of the state space. We propose an online learning algorithm that converges to SED while learning the service rates. The algorithm carefully balances empirical SED routing with forced exploration phases that guarantee sufficient sampling of both servers. We prove that our algorithm achieves finite regret; this differs from classical Multi-Armed Bandit settings where regret typically grows logarithmically in time. Finally, numerical experiments demonstrate the performance of our algorithm and highlight the regimes in which forced exploration is especially beneficial.

title: Algorithmic Optimization via Topology-Based Search
abstract: This paper introduces an algorithmic optimization method predicated on the principles of topology-based search. Traditional optimization algorithms often struggle with complex, high-dimensional problems, requiring significant computational resources and time. This research proposes a novel approach that utilizes topological concepts to intelligently guide the search process, potentially achieving greater efficiency and effectiveness in finding optimal solutions. We detail the construction of a 'Topological Search Algorithm' designed to systematically explore the solution space, leveraging the inherent structure of the problem to prioritize promising regions. The paper explores the potential benefits of this methodology, including enhanced search efficiency, improved solution quality, and the ability to address previously intractable optimization problems. We will present the implementation of this algorithm and discuss its theoretical foundations and experimental validation.

title: Adaptive Fractal Geometry for High-Dimensional Data Representation
abstract: High-dimensional data presents significant challenges for traditional data analysis and representation techniques. The 'curse of dimensionality' often leads to sparsity of information and difficulties in identifying meaningful patterns. This paper introduces a novel approach leveraging adaptive fractal geometry to address these issues. The core concept is that fractal landscapes, inherently capable of representing hierarchical and self-similar structures, can be dynamically adjusted to effectively capture the underlying distribution of high-dimensional data. We propose an algorithm that generates fractal landscapes in real-time, adapting parameters like fractal dimension (D), iteration depth (I), and scaling factor (S) based on local data density and variance. This dynamic adaptation provides a robust representation for non-stationary data, offering improved clustering, dimensionality reduction, and anomaly detection capabilities compared to static fractal methods. The algorithm's performance is evaluated through simulations and theoretical analysis, demonstrating its effectiveness in various scenarios. The key contribution lies in the real-time adaptability, moving beyond static fractal representations and offering a more nuanced and effective approach to high-dimensional data analysis.

title: Neural Network Solutions for Neural Telegraph Equations
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to solving Neural Telegraph Equations (NTEs) using deep learning. Traditional numerical methods for NTEs often struggle with accuracy and efficiency, particularly for complex systems and long time horizons. We propose a neural network architecture trained to directly approximate the solution of the NTEs, given initial conditions and time steps. The core mechanism involves mapping the input (initial state, time step) to the corresponding neural state at the output time step. abstract: This paper presents a novel quantum entanglement-based adaptive optimization algorithm designed to address complex optimization problems. The core concept revolves around exploiting the instantaneous information transfer capabilities of entangled states to guide the optimization process, thereby mitigating the pitfalls of local optima and enabling global optimization. The algorithm incorporates a dynamic parameter adjustment mechanism predicated on entanglement, allowing it to adapt to environmental changes and potentially achieve superior performance compared to traditional optimization techniques. This work explores the theoretical foundations of entanglement-based optimization and demonstrates its potential for significant advancements in the field of adaptive learning and problem-solving.

title: Quantum Entanglement Decomposition via Topological Self-Unfolding
abstract: Quantum entanglement plays a pivotal role in various quantum algorithms and quantum information processing, offering the potential for enhanced computational capabilities. However, the inherent complexity of entangled states often poses significant challenges, particularly in achieving efficient manipulation and analysis. This paper investigates a novel approach to quantum state decomposition – the Quantum Entanglement Decomposition (QED) algorithm – based on topological self-unfolding. We propose a method that leverages the inherent topological properties of quantum states to transform them into a more structured and interpretable representation, facilitating deeper understanding and computational efficiency. The core mechanism centers around creating a topological manifold within the quantum state, allowing for efficient manipulation and analysis of the underlying entanglement structure. This research introduces a new framework for quantum state decomposition, demonstrating potential advancements in the comprehension and processing of entangled quantum systems. The paper concludes with a discussion of the algorithm's theoretical foundation, experimental validation, and future research directions.

title: Dynamic Bayesian Network Inference with Compressed Sensing Techniques
abstract: This paper investigates the application of compressed sensing techniques to accelerate Bayesian network inference, particularly within the context of dynamic Bayesian networks (DBNs). Traditional Bayesian network inference methods often suffer from computational bottlenecks, especially when dealing with large and complex networks. The core idea presented here is to leverage the principles of compressed sensing – specifically, sparsity and incoherence – to dramatically reduce the computational burden of inference. We explore how compressed sensing can be integrated into the inference process, focusing on reducing the number of samples needed to accurately estimate network parameters. The approach is demonstrated through a theoretical framework, outlining the key mathematical formulations and the underlying principles. The primary focus is on the reduction of the computational complexity associated with message passing algorithms commonly used in DBN inference. The work aims to provide a viable pathway toward real-time inference in large-scale dynamic systems by offering a computationally efficient alternative. This research contributes to the growing field of hybrid Bayesian modeling and compressed sensing, with potential applications in areas such as sensor networks, time series analysis, and predictive maintenance.

title: Quantum-Based Unsupervised Feature Representation Learning
abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum computing for unsupervised feature representation learning. Traditional unsupervised methods often rely on manually designed feature extraction algorithms, limiting their applicability to complex datasets. We propose a novel approach leveraging quantum entanglement and quantum gate operations to achieve unsupervised feature extraction directly from raw data. This approach aims to enhance the generalization capability and robustness of machine learning models. The core idea involves constructing a quantum circuit-based model that implicitly maps input data and extracts relevant features through quantum entanglement and gate operations. We present a theoretical framework outlining the methodology and discuss the potential benefits and challenges of this emerging field. The primary goal is to demonstrate that quantum computing offers a fundamentally different paradigm for unsupervised learning, potentially surpassing the limitations of classical approaches. ---

title: 基于图神经网络的符号逻辑推理
abstract: This paper explores the application of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to symbolic logic reasoning. Traditional methods for symbolic logic inference often rely on heuristic algorithms and rule engines, which can be inefficient, particularly for complex logical systems. We propose a novel framework that leverages the structural representation capabilities of GNNs to model and solve symbolic logic problems effectively. The core idea involves transforming symbolic logic formulas into graph structures, enabling GNNs to learn embeddings that capture the relationships within the logic. These embeddings are then utilized to perform logical inference tasks, such as deriving new formulas or validating formula validity. This approach offers a potentially more scalable and efficient solution compared to existing methods. The key contributions of this work lie in the integration of graph representation learning with symbolic logic reasoning, providing a new computational paradigm for this long-standing problem.

title: Title: Non-Deterministic Quantum State Evolution & Reconstruction
abstract: Quantum state evolution is a fundamental challenge in quantum information processing, particularly when dealing with imperfect measurements and noisy environments. The inherent uncertainty in quantum measurements necessitates strategies for robust state reconstruction. This paper introduces a novel method for reconstructing quantum states from non-deterministic evolution, employing quantum error correction to significantly enhance fidelity. The core mechanism centers around a state reconstruction algorithm predicated on quantum error correction principles, designed to mitigate the effects of measurement errors during the initial state preparation phase. The research explores a practical implementation of this algorithm, demonstrating its ability to recover information with improved accuracy compared to conventional methods, particularly under challenging conditions. We address the core claim that this method offers a pathway to robust state reconstruction from imperfect measurement, leveraging the power of quantum error correction.

title: Title: Dynamical Constraint Optimization of Quantum Systems (DCOS) - Efficiently Optimizing Complex Quantum Algorithms
abstract: This paper introduces Dynamical Constraint Optimization of Quantum Systems (DCOS), a novel algorithm for efficiently optimizing complex quantum algorithms. Traditional methods for optimizing quantum algorithms often involve iterative adjustments of parameters, which can be time-consuming and require significant manual intervention. DCOS leverages dynamic constraints to guide the optimization process, offering a more streamlined and automated approach. The core mechanism involves iteratively adjusting parameters based on the current state of a quantum system, effectively minimizing the algorithm's cost function. We present a comprehensive theoretical analysis and a practical implementation demonstrating the effectiveness of DCOS in optimizing several key quantum algorithms. The paper details the algorithm's design, its performance compared to existing methods, and discusses potential future directions for research and development. The primary goal is to provide a robust and scalable solution for optimizing complex quantum computations, reducing the burden on researchers and developers.

title: Dynamic Key Management in Quantum Cryptography
abstract: Quantum cryptography offers unprecedented security by utilizing the laws of quantum mechanics to encrypt and transmit information. However, the inherent fragility of quantum states necessitates sophisticated key management strategies. This paper presents a novel dynamic key management algorithm for quantum cryptography, designed to automatically adjust key parameters based on evolving security requirements. We propose a method that leverages the inherent dynamism of quantum states to achieve enhanced security through continuous key adaptation. The algorithm incorporates a feedback loop that monitors security threats and dynamically modifies key variables to maintain optimal security levels. This approach aims to surpass the limitations of static key management systems, contributing to a more resilient and adaptable quantum cryptographic infrastructure. This research explores the theoretical foundations and practical implementation of this dynamic key adjustment approach, demonstrating its potential to significantly bolster the security posture of quantum communication systems.

title: Neural Network Self-Organization Driven by Information Entropy in Neuron Models
abstract: This research investigates the potential for information entropy to drive self-organization within neuron models and, consequently, within artificial neural networks. The core claim posits that fluctuations in information entropy within a neuron network can induce a dynamic process of self-organization, leading to enhanced information encoding and transmission. The proposed mechanism involves constructing a multi-layered neuron network model, continuously monitoring the entropy values of individual neurons and their connections, and leveraging the entropy increase principle alongside neuronal interactions. This process facilitates the self-organization of entropy distributions, ultimately optimizing the network's structure and functionality. Mathematical modeling explores the dynamics of entropy and its influence on network connectivity. The research contributes a novel approach to neural network design by explicitly incorporating entropy as a fundamental driver of self-organization, offering a potential pathway to more efficient and adaptive neural architectures. The study examines the theoretical underpinnings of this phenomenon and outlines a framework for future investigation.

title: Artifact for Article: Extending Deductive Verification of SYCL in VerCors with Sub-groups
abstract: Artifact for article "Extending Deductive Verification of SYCL in VerCors with Sub-groups" submitted to the STTT journal. For a full description on how to use the artifact, please see the README.md file. The artifact contains a docker image of the VerCors tool (with the described SYCL support) and documentation. Abstract of Article: SYCL is a C++ programming model for the development of heterogeneous programs. It uses the concept of kernels, where multiple instances of a computation are executed concurrently on a computing unit. This concurrency entails that the set of possible program behaviours can be of considerable size, which makes these programs error-prone. Formal verification could be used to ensure the correctness of all these possible program behaviours. In this article, SYCL support is added to VerCors, a formal verification tool for concurrent software, by encoding SYCL constructs into VerCors' internal language COL. To the extent of our knowledge, this is the first deductive verification tool for SYCL. We show how SYCL's basic- and ND-range kernels are encoded, along with the encoding and challenges related to scheduling kernels and the execution order of those kernels. Next, we discuss how SYCL's buffers and data accessors are encoded, focusing on the challenges related to it, in particular enabling memory transfer between host and device. Finally, we dicuss the encoding for sub-groups and sub-group-intrinsic functions. The usability of the added SYCL support and how it was evaluated are discussed as well.

title: Geometric interpretation of the triality relation in bipartite quantum systems
abstract: Abstract We investigate quantum correlations and coherence in bipartite systems using the universal triality relation that connects coherence, predictability, and entanglement. The geometric structure underlying entanglement in bipartite two-qubit and two-qutrit systems is analyzed using wedge products of post-measurement vectors. For two-qubit states, concurrence emerges naturally as the area spanned by the post-measurement vectors, while in qutrit systems the generalized I-concurrence is associated with higher-dimensional geometric structures formed by multiple wedge products. We further analyze the relationship between wedge products, eigenvalues, and eigenvectors of correlated systems and discuss the universality of the triality relation in arbitrary dimensions. Our results provide a geometric interpretation of entanglement in d -dimensional cases and reveal a hierarchical structure connecting low- and high-dimensional quantum systems.

title: A stage-selective transfer learning framework for small-sample quality prediction in injection molding
abstract: In small-sample injection molding quality prediction, limited target-domain data hinder stable model training, motivating transfer learning from source-domain data. However, injection molding is a multi-stage dynamic process in which injection, packing, and cooling differ in quality relevance and cross-domain feature matching, so source-domain knowledge does not have equal transfer value across stages. Existing transfer learning methods mainly rely on model parameter transfer or global feature alignment, which obscures stage-wise transfer value and dilutes target-domain-specific information. To address these limitations, this study proposes a stage-selective transfer learning framework that treats process stages as the basic transfer units. Stage transferability is evaluated by matching source-domain stage prototypes with target-domain shared features and integrated with target-domain stage importance to generate stage-selective weights. A target-domain-specific stage branch preserves intrinsic responses, while stage-level and multi-space distribution alignment constraints reduce cross-domain discrepancies. A discrepancy-aware stage attenuation mechanism further suppresses transfer and alignment contributions from severely mismatched source-domain stages. Experiments on real-world injection molding datasets show that common backbone models achieve R 2 improvements of 10.54 %–16.91 % under random splitting and 9.48 %–19.93 % under chronological splitting. Fixed-sample-size experiments confirm consistent transfer gains with only 10–100 labeled target-domain training samples, while controlled severe stage-mismatch tests demonstrate that the attenuation mechanism recovers approximately 75 % of the induced R 2 loss.

title: Modern Image Classification‐Layered Machines
abstract: The hierarchical structure of deep neural networks is neurobiologically inspired by the simple and complex cells of the visual cortex. Their layered architecture facilitates automated feature extraction, enabling pattern recognition that is invariant to translation, rotation, scaling, illumination, and distortion. This chapter introduces foundational layered machines, including Multi-layer Perceptron (MLP) and Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), covering their full training stages via error back-propagation algorithm. Furthermore, it covers various loss functions and learning algorithms for deep CNNs. The chapter also extends the unsupervised competitive learning from Chapter 17 to Self-Organizing Feature Maps (SOFMs) and variants of Learning Vector Quantization (LVQ). Practical considerations for efficient training of these networks are provided. Many realistic examples of these machines are included for various DIP tasks. The chapter ends with computer projects and challenging problems.

title: When Intelligence Becomes Agency: A Theory of Governed, Proactive Agency for Symbiotic AI Systems
abstract: Persistent AI assistants are intended to extend human attention, memory, and coordination across changing digital and physical environments. To be truly useful they must do more than just act when asked. They must decide on their own whether a situation warrants behavior at all, when it does and in what mode, whether to act, ask, monitor, defer or deliberately refrain. We call this the activation problem. Research on commitment, appraisal, mixed-initiative interaction and delegation each illuminates part of it, but none ties situated activation to continuing authorization and accountability. This paper develops a conceptual and formal framework for governed proactive agency, organizing behavior across time through perception, intent, affective-conative appraisal, constraint, and feedback. It distinguishes autonomous and delegated agency and defines symbiotic agency as delegation under a standing, revocable mandate, with continuing coupling to the principal's situation, calibrated inference of their condition, and bounded personalization. The distinctive contribution is an integrated account linking activation decisions to authorized perception, behavior selection, authority containment, traceable restraint, and constrained adaptation, with behavioral episodes as the unit of analysis. Through an agency classification method, an evaluation framework, proposed benchmark scenarios, and a reference architecture, the account provides a basis for specifying and assessing whether assistance is warranted, timely, authorized, and answerable beyond task completion alone. It is intended to guide the development and evaluation of always-present personal assistants and embodied support systems that augment human capabilities while preserving the principal's authority and judgment.

title: A Systematic Analysis of Automatic Differentiation versus Discretization-based Constraints for Physics-Informed PDE Solvers
abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) represent a growing frontier in using artificial intelligence to solve partial differential equations (PDEs). Automatic differentiation (AD) plays a central role in this paradigm, which is mesh-free and replaces traditional iterative solvers with gradient-based optimization in continuous space. However, the inherent limitations of AD, particularly in handling higher-order derivatives and discontinuous solutions, pose significant challenges for complex problems. This has motivated a growing number of researchers to explore discretization-based constraints as an alternative path. Yet, the respective applicability of these two paradigms remains largely unexplored. In this work, we conduct systematic experiments across a wide spectrum of problems, from simple linear Poisson to high-Mach hypersonic flows with strong discontinuities. Through a rigorous decomposition of approximation, optimization, and truncation errors, we systematically elucidate the fundamental trade-offs and error-governing mechanisms of both paradigms, as well as two representative network architectures: multi-layer perceptron (MLP) and graph neural network (GNN). Our results reveal a consistent trend: as nonlinearity strengthens, the accuracy advantage of discretization-based constraints becomes increasingly pronounced, with smaller optimization errors compensating for the truncation errors. Moreover, the more complex the nonlinearity and boundary conditions, the greater the advantage of GNN over MLP. These insights offer a robust practical guideline for configuring neural PDE solvers in demanding engineering applications. Our source data and code are available at https://github.com/guoxing0809/neuropde_analysis.

title: Cat-Code-Protected Controlled Quantum Communication via Non-Local CNOT Gates over Star Quantum Networks
abstract: Controlled quantum communication enables secure state transfer between a sender and receiver with the assistance of one or more controllers. However, practical implementation over optical fibre networks is severely hindered by amplitude damping, which reduces fidelity exponentially with distance. We address this challenge by combining two powerful techniques: cat-state encoding for error correction and optimal non-local CNOT gates for distributed gate implementation. The protocol eliminates the need for the physical position qubit itself to travel through the optical fibre, reducing damping events. We show, through density-matrix simulations, that our cat-code-protected protocol with a non-local CNOT operation achieves higher fidelity at 50 km, significantly outperforming the standard protocol. We analyse the protocol's security against beam-splitter attacks and show that CHSH tests provide security against beam-splitter attacks on the distributed entanglement resource despite the cat code's error correction. Our results establish that cat-code-protected controlled quantum communication is feasible with current technology and structurally extensible to multiple controllers, providing a theoretical framework for studying error-corrected controlled quantum communication over long-distance star quantum networks.

title: Contextual Observer Grounding: Evaluating Situated Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
abstract: Reasoning over language instructions in embodied tasks such as robotics often requires understanding spatial relations from a speaker's situated perspective. Humans infer such perspectives from shared environmental knowledge, activity context, and commonsense. Recent vision-language models (VLMs) appear capable of spatial reasoning, but their ability to infer a speaker's viewpoint from contextual cues and interpret situated spatial relations from that viewpoint remains unclear. We call this capability contextual observer grounding. To study this capability, we construct the Point-of-View Benchmark (POVBench), a dataset of 3D scenes and queries that disentangles Inferred, Stated, and Given forms of observer grounding in natural embodied communication. Given multi-view observations and a natural-language sentence, models must localize unseen or underspecified targets from situated spatial and contextual cues. Across state-of-the-art VLMs, localizing targets from directional language remains challenging, even when observer grounding is made explicit. We find that explicit breakdowns of observer-relative spatial reasoning improve target localization. Our project page is available at https://mimo-owl.github.io/POVBench/.

title: Task-dependent model selection for structured extraction from multilingual non-English clinical records
abstract: Abstract Objective To evaluate task-dependent selection of local and cloud models for structured extraction from multilingual non-English stroke discharge summaries, distinguishing entity detection, record assembly, and raw-document processing. Methods This retrospective system evaluation compared multilingual encoders, locally fine-tuned Qwen3-4B models, and zero-shot GPT-5.5. Primary test cohorts comprised 332 section cases, 149 medication cases with 2,475 reference records after identity-based exclusions, and 191 laboratory cases. Outcomes were section-span F1, drug-name F1, normalized seven-field record recovery, test-name F1, and laboratory quintuple F1. Paired human comparisons used a common second-annotator reference on 50 cases per task. Saved cascade outputs were compared with curated-section controls using document-bootstrap intervals. Results Section F1 was 0.919 for the encoder, 0.926 for GPT-5.5, and 0.932 for Qwen. GPT-5.5 led medication detection (0.966 versus 0.940 for Qwen), whereas Qwen led normalized medication recovery (0.381 versus 0.311; difference 0.070, 95% CI 0.026–0.114) and laboratory quintuple F1 (0.892 versus 0.822). With matched inference stacks, medication recovery declined from 0.377 on curated inputs to 0.204 for single-window and 0.246 for all-block cascades; quintuple F1 on the original laboratory cohort declined from 0.898 to 0.811. Corpus-wide extraction processed 193,101 summaries in 13.3 H100 GPU-hours. Conclusion Local models achieved strong detection performance without frontier-scale inference in this setting. Fine-tuned local LLMs were advantageous for record assembly under the evaluated recipes; annotation conventions, normalization, and upstream section extraction remained important constraints.

title: Quantum Geometry Information Encoding for High-Dimensional Data Compression and Analysis
abstract: Quantum Geometry Information Encoding (QGIEC) is a novel approach to data compression and analysis leveraging the unique properties of quantum mechanics, specifically quantum entanglement and superposition. This paper presents a method that encodes high-dimensional data within quantum bits (qubits) using quantum entanglement and superposition, aiming to achieve significantly improved compression efficiency and enhanced data analysis capabilities compared to existing techniques. The core mechanism centers around the creation of entangled states that represent data, enabling efficient manipulation and decoding through quantum algorithms. The study demonstrates the practical feasibility of QGIEC through simulations and preliminary experiments, highlighting its potential to revolutionize data storage and processing.

title: ECPC Supplementary Materials and Reproducibility Artifact for Evidence-Carrying Portability Contracts
abstract: Supplementary materials and executable reproducibility artifact supporting the manuscript "Evidence-Carrying Portability Contracts for Compiler Security Instrumentation: Differential Reconstruction of Shadow Call Stack Protocols" (manuscript information-4490441). Supplementary File S1 provides the ECPC operational specification, evidence ledger, rule-change log, and reproduction guide. Supplementary File S2 provides the version 2.1.0 standard-library Python model, eight version-pinned descriptors, authoritative rule catalogue, frozen expectation fixture, semantic tests, provenance ledger, generated matrices and witnesses, benchmark, checksums, license, and citation metadata. A fresh reference execution passes 30 semantic tests. The Compact TLS x86_64 case remains a specified design because its implementation source is unavailable; the deposit contains no performance or production-readiness claim for that configuration.

title: Dynamic Quantum State Correction: An Adaptive Error Correction Approach
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic quantum state correction algorithm designed to significantly enhance the robustness and efficiency of quantum information processing and quantum computation. Traditional error correction methods often rely on pre-computed error correction matrices, limiting their adaptability. Our approach leverages the inherent dynamic nature of quantum states to proactively detect and correct errors, overcoming the limitations of conventional techniques. The core mechanism involves a dynamically adapting quantum state transformation, enabling a more resilient and efficient error correction process. This work demonstrates the potential of this approach to improve the performance and reliability of quantum systems.

title: Cognitive Architecture and Evolutionary Algorithms: Towards Autonomous Learning Systems
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to artificial intelligence development by integrating cognitive architecture and evolutionary algorithms. The core claim is that a system combining these two paradigms can effectively facilitate autonomous learning and adaptation in AI agents. The proposed mechanism involves leveraging cognitive architecture's capabilities for knowledge representation and inference alongside the evolutionary algorithm's strengths in exploration and optimization. This hybrid system aims to overcome the limitations of traditional AI approaches that often rely on pre-programmed rules or supervised learning, which struggle with complex, dynamic environments. The presented framework offers a pathway to create more robust and flexible AI systems capable of continuous learning and adaptation without explicit human intervention. The system's architecture is described, along with key components and their interactions, outlining a potential design for a self-improving AI agent. Further research directions and potential challenges are also discussed.

title: Title: Dynamic Geometry for Adaptive Machine Learning
abstract: Dynamic Geometry for Adaptive Machine Learning addresses the limitations of static machine learning models by introducing a mechanism for dynamically adjusting geometric properties during training. This novel approach leverages quantum annealing to optimize for robustness and efficiency, ultimately enhancing generalization performance. This paper explores the potential of quantum annealing as a tool for optimizing model geometry, presenting a framework for dynamically adjusting key parameters to improve model resilience and accelerate learning. The core mechanism involves systematically exploring the space of possible model geometries using quantum annealing, while simultaneously incorporating a reinforcement learning component to guide the optimization process. We provide a detailed analysis of the proposed method, discussing its theoretical foundations and experimental validation. The paper concludes with a discussion of the implications for future research and potential applications.

title: Cognitive Graph Distillation
abstract: This paper introduces Cognitive Graph Distillation, a novel approach for extracting high-level cognitive representations from complex neural networks. The core idea is that the intricate dynamics within large neural networks can be effectively summarized by identifying and prioritizing key nodes and connections, resulting in a simplified graph representation. This distillation process leverages network influence analysis to create a graph that accurately reflects the core cognitive function. Unlike traditional methods focused on feature extraction or weight pruning, Cognitive Graph Distillation offers a fundamentally different perspective, focusing on the relational structure of the network itself. The method's potential lies in providing a means to interpret the internal workings of complex neural networks, potentially leading to new insights into the mechanisms of cognition. We detail the algorithm, its key components, and discuss its potential applications.

title: Self-Adaptive Geometric Transformation Optimization via Quantum Computing
abstract: This paper introduces a novel optimization algorithm based on quantum computing designed to efficiently find optimal geometric transformations. Traditional optimization methods often struggle with complex geometric problems, while quantum computing offers the potential for significantly faster and more accurate solutions. We propose a framework that leverages quantum superposition and entanglement to accelerate the search process and enhance the precision of geometric transformations. The core mechanism involves a hybrid quantum-classical approach, utilizing quantum algorithms to explore the solution space and classical optimization techniques to refine the results. This work demonstrates the feasibility of applying quantum computing to geometric optimization, presenting a new approach with the potential to revolutionize the field. The proposed algorithm is designed to be scalable and adaptable to a wide range of geometric transformations.

abstract: This paper investigates the potential of quantum acceleration for solving complex geometric transformations, specifically focusing on non-linear geometric mappings. Traditional computational methods often struggle with the inherent complexity and time-consuming nature of these transformations. Quantum computing offers a fundamentally different approach, leveraging quantum entanglement and superposition to perform calculations with potentially exponential speedups. We explore a novel quantum algorithm designed to accelerate the transformation of geometric primitives, aiming to significantly enhance computational efficiency. This work presents a detailed analysis of the algorithm's design, potential challenges, and preliminary results demonstrating improvements in computational speed compared to classical methods for a specific, representative geometric mapping. The core claim emphasizes the significant impact of quantum acceleration on these tasks, highlighting the algorithm's ability to streamline complex computations.

title: Probability Logic Framework for Adaptive Performance (PL-ADF)
abstract: This paper presents a novel probabilistic logic framework, termed PL-ADF, designed to enhance the adaptability of algorithms through dynamic parameter adjustment based on observed data and environmental changes. Traditional probabilistic models often require manual parameter tuning, while PL-ADF aims to automate this process, leading to improved algorithm robustness and performance. The core innovation lies in an adaptive parameter adjustment algorithm that learns from data and adjusts parameters to maintain optimal performance across varying inputs. This paper introduces the algorithm, outlines its implementation, and discusses its potential applications across diverse domains. The work focuses on achieving a level of adaptability surpassing static parameter adjustment techniques.

title: Cognitive Computing with Semantic Web Technologies and Bayesian Networks
abstract: Current cognitive computing systems often struggle with genuine understanding, relying heavily on pattern recognition and statistical correlations rather than robust semantic comprehension. This paper proposes a novel approach to cognitive computing that addresses this limitation by integrating the strengths of semantic web technologies, specifically Resource Description Framework (RDF) and Web Ontology Language (OWL), with Bayesian Networks. The core idea is to leverage the formal representation of knowledge provided by the semantic web alongside the probabilistic reasoning capabilities of Bayesian Networks. This combined framework allows the system to not only identify patterns but also to reason about complex concepts and relationships, incorporating prior knowledge and explicitly accounting for uncertainty. The architecture presented here offers a significant step towards creating cognitive systems that more closely resemble human thought processes, capable of contextual understanding and adaptive reasoning. We outline the key components of the system and discuss the potential benefits of this integrated approach.
